ox: Incorrect. At 1 hour the table shows no high values; the large concentrations are at 4 h. The passage states the peak (Tmax) is about 4.5 h, not 1 h.
Correct. Concentrations climb from 0 at baseline to a peak around 4 h (2.8–4.0 in the table; passage says Cmax at 4.5 h) and then fall by 8 h (about 1.0–1.5).
Incorrect. The values change a lot (0.0 → about 3.5 → about 1.2), so concentration is not constant.
Incorrect. There is a clear change over time, so 'no change' contradicts the table.

p: For a trend question, compare the first, middle and last values. A rise then a fall is a peak shape. Pharmacokinetics: Cmax is the peak concentration and Tmax is the time it occurs.

bp1034_0.trap: Option A suggests a rapid rise at 1 hour, which neither the table nor the passage supports.
mem: Cmax = highest concentration; Tmax = time of that peak.
Trend = look at start, middle and end values.
Oral drugs usually take hours to peak.
bp1034_0.sc: Check three points: start (0), middle (high), end (lower) → up then down.
bp1034_0.mn: C-max = Crest, T-max = Time of the crest.
bp1034_0.plain: Imagine a bathtub: the drug pours in (rising), then drains out (falling). The highest water level is the peak.

ox: Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays bound to the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. High glucose also keeps cAMP low. Transcription is off.
Wrong. Lactose releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low, so CAP is not activated. You get only low-level transcription. Trap: thinking lactose alone is enough.

Correct. Lactose becomes allolactose, which binds the repressor and releases it from the operator. Low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and helps RNA polymerase bind. Both signals together give maximum transcription.
Wrong. With no lactose, the repressor stays on the operator. Low glucose would make CAP active, but the gene is still blocked.

p: The lac operon holds genes to digest lactose. It has two controls. A repressor protein blocks the gene unless lactose (as allolactose) is present. That is negative control.

CAP is an activator. It works only when cAMP is high, which happens when glucose is low. That is positive control. Bacteria prefer glucose, so they switch on lactose genes fully only when lactose is present and glucose is gone.

mem: Lactose present: repressor off the operator
Glucose low: cAMP high: CAP active
Max expression needs lactose present AND glucose absent
q10.trap: Stopping once the repressor is released. You also need CAP activation, which needs low glucose.
q10.plain: A light turns on only if two switches are both on: 'there is food I can use' and 'my favorite food is gone'.

ox: Wrong. No known DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 5' end. The direction is 5' to 3'. Trap: confusing the direction of the template read with the direction of the new strand.
Correct. DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3'-OH of the growing strand. So the new strand grows 5' to 3'. It reads the template 3' to 5'.
Wrong. Both leading and lagging strands are built 5' to 3'. The lagging strand just has to be built in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.
Wrong. DNA polymerase cannot start from nothing. It needs a primer, made of RNA by primase, to provide a free 3'-OH.

p: DNA strands have two different ends, called 5' and 3'. DNA polymerase can only attach a new nucleotide to the 3' end of an existing strand. So the new strand always grows from 5' toward 3'.
It also cannot start on its own. It needs a short RNA primer that gives it a 3'-OH to build on.

mem: New DNA is made 5' to 3'
Polymerase needs a primer with a free 3'-OH
Lagging strand makes Okazaki fragments
q7.trap: Mixing up the template direction (read 3' to 5') with the direction of new synthesis (5' to 3').
q7.plain: Building a train where you can only add cars to the back. You can never add to the front, and you need a first car already in place.

ox: Wrong. Helicase unwinds the double helix. That unwinding is what creates the positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Trap: helicase causes the problem; it does not fix it.
Correct. Topoisomerase cuts one or both DNA strands, lets the DNA swivel to release tension, and then reseals the cut. This relieves the supercoiling.
Wrong. Ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, such as between Okazaki fragments. It does not release twisting strain.
Wrong. Primase makes short RNA primers so that polymerase can start. It has no role in supercoiling.

p: When helicase unwinds a stretch of DNA, the DNA ahead gets overwound and tight. This is called positive supercoiling. If it builds up, replication stalls.
Topoisomerase solves this. It briefly cuts the DNA, lets it spin to relax, and reseals it. In bacteria, gyrase is a topoisomerase targeted by some antibiotics.

mem: Helicase unwinds
Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling by cutting and rejoining
Primase makes RNA primers; ligase seals nicks
q8.trap: Picking helicase because it is at the fork. It creates the strain; topoisomerase removes it.
q8.plain: If you pull two twisted rope strands apart, the rope ahead of you gets twisted tighter. Someone has to snip, untwist, and tie it back.

ox: Wrong. A silent mutation changes the codon but still codes for the same amino acid. UAG codes for no amino acid, so this is not silent.
Wrong. Missense means a different amino acid is inserted. Here no amino acid is inserted. UAG is a stop signal.
Correct. UAG is a stop codon. Changing UAC (Tyr) to UAG ends translation early, so the protein is truncated. That is a nonsense mutation.
Wrong. A frameshift comes from adding or removing bases (not in multiples of 3), shifting every codon after it. Here one base was swapped, so the frame is intact.

p: A codon is three RNA bases that code for one amino acid. A point mutation swaps one base. Silent: same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid. Nonsense: a stop codon appears.
The stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA. If one appears early, translation ends early and the protein is shorter, usually non-functional.

mem: Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA
Silent: same amino acid; missense: different; nonsense: stop
Frameshift needs an insertion or deletion not divisible by 3
q9.mn: Stop codons: 'U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away' for UAA, UAG, UGA.
q9.trap: Calling it missense because one amino acid is replaced. Here it is replaced by a stop signal, not another amino acid.
q9.plain: A sentence with a typo that makes a different word is missense. A typo that puts a period in the middle of the sentence is nonsense: the sentence stops early.

ox: Wrong. A placebo control gives a comparison for the drug effect but does not reduce differences between people.

Correct. In a crossover design, each subject gets both treatments (Compound Y and placebo, with a 14-day washout between), so each person acts as their own control. Differences between people then cancel out of the comparison.
Wrong. Double-blinding hides who gets which treatment, which prevents bias, not person-to-person variability.
Wrong. Randomization (the order of treatments) prevents systematic bias, but it does not remove natural differences between people.

p: In a crossover trial, every person gets each treatment, one after another, in random order. A washout period between them lets the first drug leave the body.
Since the same person is compared with themselves, differences like body size and metabolism do not affect the comparison.

bp1034_1.plain: It is like testing two pairs of running shoes on the same runner, instead of giving each shoe to a different runner.
mem: Crossover = each subject is their own control.
Washout = drug-free gap between treatments.
Blinding reduces bias, not variability.
bp1034_1.trap: Choosing double-blind or randomization; they address bias, not variability between subjects.

ox: Wrong. 0.07 h⁻¹ would give a half-life of about 10 hours (0.7/0.07 = 10), not 2.5 hours.
Wrong. 0.14 h⁻¹ would give a half-life of about 5 hours (0.7/0.14 = 5).
Wrong. 0.35 h⁻¹ would give a half-life of about 2 hours (0.7/0.35 = 2), slightly short of 2.5.
Correct. k = 0.693 / t½ = 0.693 / 2.5, which is about 0.7 / 2.5 = 0.28 h⁻¹. The passage gives t½ = 2.5 hours. The AUC of 18.6 is not needed.

p: First-order elimination means the body removes a fixed fraction of the drug each hour. The rate constant k is that fraction per hour.
Half-life (t½) is the time for the concentration to fall by half. They are linked by k = 0.693 / t½.

bp1034_2.plain: It is like a leaky tire losing the same percent of air each hour: a quicker half-life means a bigger k.
mem: Short half-life = large k.
Use 0.7 for no-calculator work.

fm.f: k = ln(2) / t½, where k = elimination rate constant (per hour), ln(2) = 0.693, t½ = half-life in hours
fm.why: For first-order elimination, half-life and k are inversely related.

bp1034_2.sc: Dividing by 2.5 is the same as multiplying by 0.4.
bp1034_2.trap: Using the AUC in the calculation. It is a distractor; only t½ is needed.

ox: Wrong. The passage says the data suggest 'a moderate absorption rate,' so this is supported.
Wrong. The passage states 'No serious adverse events were reported,' so this is supported.
Correct. The passage gives 'apparent elimination half-life (t½) was 2.5 hours,' so a half-life longer than 9 hours is not supported.
Wrong. The passage says Cmax ranged 'from 1.8 to 4.6 µg/mL,' so Cmax varied between subjects.

p: Check each statement against the passage. Three will be directly backed by passage text. The one that is not is the answer.
A single number in the passage can be enough to disprove a statement.

bp1034_3.plain: It is like comparing four claims against a receipt; the one that does not match the receipt is the wrong one.
mem: Find the exact passage line for each option.
Half-life is not the same as Tmax.
Cmax range shows variability.
bp1034_3.trap: Assuming a long half-life because the peak comes late. Tmax is 4.5 h but t½ is only 2.5 h.

ox: Wrong. Cmax is a single peak value after one dose. It does not capture the total exposure that determines the average level on repeated dosing.
Wrong. Tmax tells when the peak occurs, which describes absorption speed, not how high the steady-state level will be.

Correct. AUC measures total drug exposure from one dose, which equals dose divided by clearance (with bioavailability). The average steady-state concentration depends on the same quantity, so AUC (18.6 µg·h/mL here) is the best predictor.
Wrong. Half-life affects how fast steady state is reached and how much drug accumulates, but AUC captures the overall exposure that sets the level.

p: AUC is the area under the concentration-time curve, a measure of how much drug the body is exposed to. It reflects how well the body clears the drug.
At steady state, the average concentration depends on dose per interval and clearance. Since AUC reflects the same clearance, it predicts the steady-state level.

bp1034_4.plain: It is like total water in a tub over time: what stays in depends on how much comes in and how fast it drains.
mem: AUC reflects exposure and clearance.
Cmax = peak, Tmax = peak time.
t½ affects time to reach steady state (about 4 to 5 half-lives).
bp1034_4.trap: Choosing t½ because it relates to accumulation; it sets timing, not the level.
